source.work: Doris Stevens, Jailed for Freedom (1920), Appendix 4: Suffrage Prisoners

add.name: Rose Fishstein
add.description:
Rose Fishstein was a Philadelphia businesswoman and a member of the National Woman's Party, one of the "Silent Sentinels" imprisoned during the 1917-1919 campaign to picket the Wilson White House for woman suffrage. She was born in Russia, educated in New York and Philadelphia, and was a student at Temple University. She was arrested at a watchfire demonstration in February 1919 and sentenced to five days in the District Jail.

She was the sister-in-law of Rose Gratz Fishstein, who is also in this archive. Doris Stevens lists the two women as separate entries in Appendix 4 of Jailed for Freedom, one immediately after the other, and the shared forename and surname are why this record was missing: every automatic check for Rose Fishstein found Rose Gratz Fishstein and stopped.

cases.charges: Arrested for picketing the Wilson White House for woman suffrage.
cases.convicted: Imprisoned in the 1917-1919 National Woman's Party suffrage campaign
cases.sentence:
Five days in the District Jail, which is the sentence Doris Stevens records.

NO DAY IS STORED, only the month. Stevens gives "Feb., 1919" for her where she gives February 9 for her sister-in-law, so neither the day she was taken in nor the day she came out is established. The women arrested at the February 9 watchfire demonstration were released together on February 13 after the hunger strike, which means the five days imposed may well not be the time actually served. The row carries a month-precision incarceration and no release date, and publishes no imprisonment figure.

duplicate.why:
Stevens lists one Mrs. Lawrence Lewis. The archive carries two records for her, and they disagree with each other: dora-lewis gives born 1862-06-12, died 1928-10-22; dora-kelly-lewis gives born 1862-10-13, died 1928-01-31. Both describe the same Philadelphia widow, the same Night of Terror at Occoquan on November 14, 1917. dora-kelly-lewis also holds a case row whose incarceration date (July 6, 1917) precedes its arrest date (November 9, 1917), which is the mismatched-pair shape the duration guard discards.

NOT MERGED HERE. Merging means choosing which birth and death dates to keep, and neither record says where its dates came from. That is a research question, not a script.
